tip: 'Problema' is masculine even though it ends in '-a': 'o problema', not 'a problema'. Same for 'tema', 'sistema', 'programa'.
As slang for guy, 'cara' is masculine: 'aquele cara'. The everyday word 'a cara' means face.
Use 'está' (from 'estar') for changing conditions like traffic: 'como está o trânsito' asks about right now, not a fixed trait.
Ask a name with 'qual é', not 'o que': 'qual é o seu nome'. Portuguese uses 'which is' where English reaches for 'what'.
'Quando' = when. Portuguese questions often keep statement word order: 'Quando você chega?' not 'Quando chega você?'
'Posso' is I can or may, from 'poder'. 'Posso' plus an infinitive asks for permission: 'onde posso estacionar'.
'Assinar' means to sign, but it also means to subscribe: 'eu assino a revista'. Same verb, two senses.
'Falou' (literally 'spoke') is a casual goodbye in Brazil, like 'later' or 'peace out.' Often combined: 'falou, valeu!'
'Pessoa' is grammatically feminine no matter who it refers to: 'aquela pessoa', even when the person is a man.
'Quem' (who) normally takes a singular verb even when the answer is many people: 'Quem fez esse bolo?' = who made this cake?
In 'vocês se mudaram', 'mudar' with 'se' means to move (house); 'mudar' alone means to change.
'Trouxe' is the irregular past of 'trazer' (to bring): 'quem trouxe o bolo' = who brought the cake.
'Por que' (two words) is used in questions. 'Porque' (one word) is for answers. This is one of the trickiest spelling rules in Portuguese.
'Quando é' = when is. 'Aniversário' is used for both birthday and anniversary in Portuguese.
In Brazil, 'tem' commonly means there is or there are: 'onde tem' = where is there. The textbook word 'há' is rare in speech.
'A gente' means we but takes a singular verb: 'a gente pode', never 'a gente podemos'.
'Estar' plus the '-ndo' form is the right-now '-ing': 'está lendo' means you are reading. Brazilians use it more than the simple present.
'Feriado' is a public holiday, a single day off. Vacation time is 'férias', which is always plural.
Make comparisons with 'mais' before the adjective: 'mais rápido' = faster. Portuguese has no '-er' ending like English.
The 'é que' in 'como é que isso funciona' is just filler that sounds natural; it means the same as 'como isso funciona'.
'Qual é a senha' = what's the password. 'Senha' means password, PIN, or queue number in Brazil.
Present-tense 'volta' covers near-future plans, so 'Quando você volta?' means when are you coming back, not just when do you return now.
'Ir' plus an infinitive is the everyday future: 'vão casar' = are going to get married. No separate future tense needed.
'Para cá' means to here or over here, moving toward the speaker: 'veio para cá' = came over here. 'Cá' usually pairs with motion verbs.
'A gente' literally means the people but works as informal we, and it takes a singular verb: 'a gente se encontra', never 'encontramos'.
'Daqui' = 'de' + 'aqui' (from here). Similar contractions: 'dali' ('de' + 'ali'), 'daí' ('de' + 'aí'), 'daquele' ('de' + 'aquele').
Brazil takes an article: 'no Brasil' is 'em' plus 'o Brasil'. Many countries do ('o Brasil', 'os EUA'), but Portugal takes none.
After a measure, use plain 'de' with no article: 'um litro de leite', 'uma xícara de café'.
Brazilians usually put the object pronoun before the verb: 'me incomoda' = bothers me, not the European 'incomoda-me'.
Descriptive adjectives normally follow the noun: 'computador novo' = new computer, not 'novo computador'.
